note.saw: In the opening sketch the autumn leaves read as flat coins and polka dots, the right tree was a stack of dots with no branches, and the sun glow was small and half hidden by the far shore. The clouds were thin pale smears and the water lines too even and bright.
note.changing: Leaves become ragged, torn-edged brush clumps, the right tree gets scratched-in branches, the sun grows into a big near-white glow with a wider gold shaft below it, and the clouds fill out with gold lower edges. The reflections soften into wide streaks and the ripple lines break up.
note.why: Bob Ross's autumn trees are tapped clumps with torn edges, not stamps, and the whole picture lives on its one column of light, so that has to be the strongest thing in it.
note.idea: A glass-still autumn lake at sunset: the horizon a little under the middle, one pale sun-glow just right of centre warming outward through orange and crimson to a violet top, a dark headland with a little cabin on the left, one tall near-black tree on the right, and the lake repeating it all upside down with a single golden column pulled straight down.

note.saw: The sun sat like a flat grey-white dome over a pale lavender far shore, and every bush was spangled with gold top to bottom as if lit from behind the viewer. The gold path in the water was a picket fence of separate bars, dimmest right at the shoreline.
note.changing: Every clump of leaves is rebuilt as backlit: a dark plum-brown body with gold only as a thin rim facing the sun. The water glow becomes one joined patch, near-white under the horizon and narrowing to amber, the far trees turn dark blue-violet, a dark veil falls over the reflections, and the headland gets two autumn trees on grounded trunks.
note.why: The sun is behind everything, so light should only kiss the edges and whatever stands in front of it should go dark; that contrast is what makes a sunset burn.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's first suggestions, since each one fixes the same mistake: light coming from the wrong place.

note.saw: The backlighting worked, but the far tree line ran straight through the sun, so the brightest spot was in the water, not the sky. The clouds were thin airbrushed streaks, the bushes were round coin-like dabs, and the strokes across the gold column were evenly ruled dashes.
note.changing: A hot near-white sun now sits half sunk on the far tree line, with the trees dipping lower and darker in front of it. The clouds become fuller criss-cross masses with gold only on the bellies nearest the sun, every bush is rebuilt from little fans of bristle taps, and the water gets tapered, uneven strokes instead of ruled dashes.
note.why: A Bob Ross sunset needs one place the eye can't leave, and that has to be the sun at the horizon with its reflection pulled straight down below it; everything else should read as brush and knife, not dots and rulers.

note.saw: The sun was a dull, greyish dome under the canvas grain, so the white patch in the water outshone the sun that made it. The headland reflections hung with dark sticks like a barcode, the left water had gone muddy brown, the shoreline cut was equally bright edge to edge, and the front bank was a big dark wedge with a dotted gold outline.
note.changing: A small near-white, yellow-hearted sun is painted on top of the grain, half sunk behind the darkest far trees, with the water patch pulled down to warm gold. The shoreline cut glows brightest under the sun and fades at the sides, the barcode sticks become soft wide pulls over plum-violet water, the tall tree gets its own little autumn bank, and the front bank shrinks into separate bushes.
note.why: Water gives back a little less light than it gets, so the brightest spot has to be the sun itself with the lake a quieter echo. The owner's note about smooth paint is why the reflections become soft pulls and the bank loses its hard outline.
note.visionary: Takes all four of the critic's newest suggestions, because each one makes the light come from one place.

note.saw: This is the first artist's finished painting, rendered again as the starting point for a fresh pair of eyes.
note.changing: Nothing visible changes yet; the painting is looked at whole, at full size and up close, before any repainting begins.
note.why: A second artist studies the inherited picture first so the list of what to fix comes from what is actually on the canvas.
note.idea: Coming in fresh, the second artist sees the right mood but the wrong paint: a canvas-grain speckle covers everything like TV static, the column is a foggy beige curtain with drippy comb teeth, the horizon has no depth behind it, the autumn trees look like glitter on stickers, and the tall tree is round clumps on a pole. The plan is to make it smooth, wet and layered the way Bob Ross paints.

note.saw: The picture looked smooth, but the autumn trees and front bank were dotted with round yellow blossoms, the column had straight sides like a spotlight, fine vertical hairlines drizzled over the lake like rain past a window, and thin spires stuck up from the far shore like a town skyline.
note.changing: Autumn highlights tone down to soft ochre and sienna, the column becomes a narrow hot core inside wide, feathered pulls, the hairline rain gives way to broad plum and rose glazes, and the far shore gets rounded tips. The pine is rebuilt as drooping fan-brush tiers with sky between them, and a warm mist gathers at the foot of the headland and the pine.
note.why: Still water and a dim evening sky are the smoothest things in a Bob Ross painting, and that calm is what makes the one hot column read as light.
note.visionary: Takes all three of the critic's newest notes (smooth the lake, feather the column, melt the sky's hatching) plus its earlier mist idea, but turns down keeping the gold flowers on the front bank because at full size they read as blossoms.

note.saw: The lake read as still glass, but the sun had a faint ring around it like a lamp shade, the knife highlights under it had gone blurry, the headland trees were an even carpet of maroon petals, and the pine's tiers sat like shelves around a hard trunk line.
note.changing: The ring melts into one smooth bloom, and four or five crisp, warm, tapered knife cuts lie flat just under the sun. Each autumn tree gets a rounded body with a warm sun side and a deeper shadow side, the headland slope rolls in soft curved strokes with rose-gold mist at its foot, and the pine gets uneven tiers with its trunk hidden among them.
note.why: In Bob Ross's evenings the crispest marks live right where the sun touches the water, and everything else stays soft so that spot sings; rounded trees with lit and shadow sides read as real bushes, not wallpaper. The owner's call for smooth brushstrokes everywhere is why the slope strokes become curves.

visions.seen: Oh, that's a warm evening, friend. The sky melts from violet down into orange like it was blended wet-on-wet, and that little cabin window glowing on the hill makes me want to sit on the porch. But the sun is behind everything here, and right now the trees are lit as if it were shining from over my shoulder.
suggestions: The front bank in the lower left and the headland with the cabin: the gold dabs are spread evenly over the whole bush, top to bottom. With the sun low and straight ahead, the sides facing us sit in shadow. Maybe keep the brightest gold taps only on the top edges, the side toward the sun, as a thin rim of light, and let the lower front of each clump drop into dark plum-brown with only a few dull ochre taps. The tall pine on the right could get the same: a warm rim on its sun-facing left edge and darker clumps on the right. That one change will make the sun feel like it's really behind the trees.

The gold path in the water under the sun: right now it reads as separate vertical bars with dark gaps between them, and it's dimmer right at the shoreline than further down. Reflected light is brightest just under the horizon. You might let it start as a wide, near-white patch right under the sun, then narrow and warm to gold and amber as it comes toward us, and cross it with a few thin horizontal swipes of light, the way Bob pulls the color straight down and then barely touches it sideways. Water that still shows a glassy, joined-up glow, not a picket fence.

The sun itself and the far shore under it: the sun is a pale, nearly gray-white dome and the far shore beneath it is a light lavender strip. Picture a hot yellow-white core with a soft warm halo that bleeds over and eats the top edge of the far trees, and those far trees turned into a soft blue-violet silhouette, a touch darker right under the sun. Things in front of the light go darker, not lighter, and that contrast makes the sun burn.

The reflections of the headland and the pine: they match the real trees almost value for value. Reflections in still water come back a little darker and a little greyer than what they mirror. A thin, darker veil over those reflected shapes would put the land on the land and the water in the water.
visions.keep: The violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky and its soft clouds, the cabin's lit window, the thin bright cut where the shore meets the water, the deep plum water in the bottom right corner, and the way the pine's reflection softens as it comes down. That's all good painting.

visions.seen: Now that's a sunset sinking behind the trees, friend: the far shore went dark violet and the sun is burning through it, and the leaves only catch fire on their edges. You took all four of my last notes and the whole lake feels quieter and truer for it, but the sky has lost its fire while the water kept it, and my eye now lives in the lake instead of the sky.
suggestions: The sun behind the far tree line, center just below the horizon: the hot core is almost gone, so the patch in the water reads brighter than the sky that makes it. Water gives back a little less than it gets. Maybe let a small near-white, yellow-hearted half disc peek up between the dark far treetops right above the glow in the water, with a tight bright halo around it, and pull the water's white patch down a step toward warm gold so the brightest spot in the whole painting is the sun itself.

The thin cream clouds across the upper sky: they're all one pale color with soft edges everywhere, like the light hits them from nowhere. With the sun low and below them, only their undersides catch it. You might give each one a hot gold or peach lower edge on the side toward the sun, let their tops cool into dusty mauve that nearly melts into the sky, and make the ones lowest and nearest the sun the brightest while the high ones at top left go rose and dim. That's how Bob's clouds get their bellies lit.

The bright white line where the shore meets the water, running edge to edge: it's equally bright under the dark headland on the left and under the big pine on the right. Light only skims the water where it can see the sun. Perhaps let that line glow strongest in the middle where the sun sits, fade to a thin dim ochre toward both sides, and break or nearly vanish under the darkest trees.

The headland's reflection, left side of the lake: it still has a row of dark, hard vertical sticks hanging in it like a barcode, sharper than the soft trees they mirror. A few soft, wide, blurred pulls (darker plum, edges fading), with one or two thin sideways swipes of pale light cutting across them, would read as glassy water instead of posts standing in it.
visions.keep: The new dark violet far shore with the sun bleeding through it, the backlit leaves with gold only on their rims, the joined column of light in the water that narrows as it comes toward us, the darker veil over the reflections, the cabin's little lit window and the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky.

visions.seen: Ah, there's the sun now, friend, a warm half disc easing down behind the far trees, and the clouds have gone soft and wet like they were blended right into the sky. You took the sun and the soft headland reflection to heart, and the whole upper half breathes; it's the few stiff, hard edges left in the lake and on the pine that still catch my eye like a pencil line on a wet canvas.
suggestions: The gold column in the water, center, especially its lower half: it breaks into separate vertical strings that end in ragged, comb-like teeth around the bottom third. Picture it as one soft wet-on-wet pull instead: blend the strands into each other with wide, semi-transparent strokes, and let the bottom simply melt away into the plum water with no visible ends. Light on still water fades, it doesn't drip, and a smooth column will read as glass the way Bob's do.

The tall pine on the right, its top and right edge: thin straight black lines poke out from the trunk like wires or antennae, ruler-straight and hard. You might let those become soft fan-brush branch tips that droop a little and taper out, dark plum blending into the sky at their ends, with just a whisper of gold on the sun-facing left tips. The tree is backlit, so its edges should be soft and glowing, not cut.

The front bank in the lower left: a thin pale line traces its whole curved edge down to the bottom of the picture, like an outline drawn around it. Maybe keep a bright cut only on the short stretch nearest the sun, where the light can actually skim the water, and let the rest of the edge sink softly into its own dark reflection. Then those scattered gold specks along its top could gather into a few rounder, softer tapped clumps so the bank reads as paint, not glitter.
visions.keep: The half-sunk sun with its warm halo over the dark far trees, the soft melted clouds, the wide soft pulls in the headland's reflection, the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky, the backlit rims on the leaves, and the cabin's little lit window.

visions.seen: This one sits quiet as a held breath, friend: the sun is resting on the far trees and the whole lake drinks its amber. You took the hot little sun and the softer headland reflection to heart, but the air around the sun still feels sandy and static, as if the glow were sprinkled on instead of blended in, and the land and water meet with no air between them.
suggestions: The glow around the sun, center just above the horizon: the bright halo is speckled with grain like sand on the canvas, and it stays small. Maybe let the canvas texture fade right out over that area and lay two or three wide, smooth, semi-transparent rings instead: a pale lemon heart, then warm peach, then a wide soft apricot that melts into the orange sky well past the cloud bellies. The brightest light in a painting is the smoothest thing in it, and a wider soft bloom will make the sun truly radiate, the way Bob blends his yellow glow with big criss-cross strokes before anything else goes on.

Where the land meets the water, along the foot of the cabin headland on the left and the foot of the tall pine on the right: the dark land drops straight into the dark water with no air between them, and the headland's slope down to the water is one long straight diagonal. You might tap in a thin, soft band of warm, hazy mist along those bases (a dusty rose-gold, brightest toward the sun, almost gone at the outer edges), and let the headland's slope roll in a few gentle bumps of bushes instead of one ruled line. Bob always mists the bottom of his trees; that little veil of lit air puts distance between the planes and makes the evening feel humid and still.

The far tree line under the sun, the thin strip between the headland and the pine: its tops read like small square blocks, almost a little city skyline. Perhaps let it become a row of soft, rounded and pointed fan-brush tips, uneven in height, cool blue-violet and a touch darker than the sky right next to them, dissolving into the sun's halo where they overlap. Distant trees are only soft shapes in the haze, and a softer edge there will match the owner's wish for smooth paint.
visions.keep: The small near-white sun with its yellow heart sitting half sunk, the hot cloud bellies near the sun with their dusty mauve tops, the shoreline cut that is brightest under the sun and fades at the sides, the soft wide pulls in the headland's reflection, the backlit gold rims, the cabin's lit window and the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky. My last notes on the comb-like lower end of the gold column and the wire-like twigs on the pine still stand as offers if they speak to you.

visions.seen: Oh, now that's a soft evening, friend: the sun is a little white coal resting in the trees and its light pours down the lake in one wide, warm pull that melts away instead of dripping. You let the column fade out and the far trees go hazy, and it breathes. What still pulls me out is a fine rain of thin scratches over the water and the sky, like the canvas is being drizzled on.
suggestions: The whole lake, left and right of the gold column: thin, hair-fine vertical streaks run down the water everywhere, so the lake reads like rain falling past a window. Still water is the smoothest thing in a Bob Ross painting. You might blend those away into broad, soft plum and rose glazes, keeping only the few wide pulled-down reflection strokes, and let three or four thin, pale sideways swipes do the work of showing it's water. A smooth mirror lets the reflected light read as light, not texture, and it answers the owner's wish for smooth, wet paint.

The sides of the gold column, center of the lake: its left and right edges run down like straight, hard walls, most clearly on the right side about halfway down. Picture those edges feathered out into the plum water with wide, semi-transparent strokes, so the glow fades sideways as softly as it now fades at the bottom, with the warmest, brightest part held in a narrow core right under the sun. Light on glassy water has no edges; it simply grows dimmer the farther it strays from the sun's line.

The upper sky, especially the violet top and both upper corners: a fine diagonal hatching still scratches across the clouds and color. Maybe let those strokes melt into big, soft, criss-cross blends where you can no longer see single lines, keeping the cloud shapes but losing the scratches. A dim twilight sky is pure air, and smooth, wet blending there will make the bright center feel even hotter by contrast.
visions.keep: The small near-white sun half sunk in the soft, hazy far trees, the wide warm bloom around it, the gold column that now melts away at the bottom with no comb teeth, the cloud bellies lit gold near the sun with dusty mauve tops, the shoreline cut brightest under the sun, the backlit gold rims on the leaves, the gold flowers tapped on the front bank, the cabin's lit window and the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky.

visions.seen: Now the lake is a true mirror, friend: you blended away the hairline rain, feathered the sides of the gold column and melted the sky's scratches, and the water lies still as glass. What catches me now is the sun's glow, drawn as rings like ripples on a target, and a few thin, ruler-straight dark lines that still stand stiff against all that soft paint.
suggestions: The glow around the sun, center just above the far trees: it shows two or three visible round edges, like the rings of a target or a pale rainbow, each one stepping down in brightness. Light in the air never has edges. Maybe blend those rings into one smooth bloom that fades evenly from the lemon-white heart out into the orange sky, with no line where one ring ends and the next begins, the way Bob scrubs his yellow glow in big soft criss-cross strokes until you can't find where it stops.

The tall pine on the right and its reflection: a thin, straight dark trunk line shows through the gaps between the tiers from top to bottom, and in the water it runs on as one hard dark line nearly to the bottom of the picture. Perhaps let the trunk hide behind the tiers, showing only in a few short soft glimpses, and in the reflection let it soften, break up and fade out halfway down, crossed by two or three pale sideways swipes. A reflection is quieter and blurrier than the tree it mirrors, and the line would stop pulling the eye away from the sun.

The front bank in the lower left: thin dark grass stalks stick up out of the gold bushes like bent wires, and a few spiky ones stand near its lower edge. You might turn them into a handful of soft, rounded dark taps and short curved pulls that melt into the bush shapes, with a touch of warm rim only on the tops facing the sun. That bank is the nearest thing to us and the darkest; soft, quiet shapes there frame the glowing lake instead of scratching across it.

The slope below the cabin on the left headland, just above the gold bushes near the water: a few thin, straight dark posts stand up like a little fence. Maybe soften them into one or two small rounded bushes, dark plum with a gold rim on their sun side, so the slope rolls down to the water in soft shapes like everything around it.
visions.keep: The glassy, smooth lake, the feathered gold column with its hot narrow core that melts away at the bottom, the soft wet sky with gold-bellied clouds near the sun, the small near-white sun half sunk in the hazy blue-violet far trees, the warm mist at the foot of the pine, the drooping fan-brush tiers of the pine, the soft blurred headland reflection, the cabin's lit window and the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky.

visions.seen: Ah, friend, the sun finally breathes: you melted the rings into one smooth bloom and laid those crisp little knife cuts flat on the water right under it, and now that's the spot my eye can't leave. What still tugs at me is the tall pine on the right, where the light on its branches looks stamped on rather than caught.
suggestions: The tall pine on the right, the left tips of its tiers: every tier ends in the same little stack of bright orange bars, like the rungs of a ladder, top to bottom. The sun sits low and to the left of the tree, so the light really only catches the lower tiers, the ones closest to the glow. You might turn those bars into a few soft, rounded taps of muted ochre and burnt sienna, warmest on the bottom three or four tiers, then let them thin out and cool into dusky rose higher up, until the top tiers against the violet sky are dark silhouette with no rim at all. Light that fades as it climbs shows where the sun really is.

The lowest tier of the pine, just above the little autumn bank at its foot: it bends into an arch with bright sky showing through underneath, so it reads like a small bridge or doorway. Maybe fill that opening with a soft, dark, bushy mass, the way Bob lets the bottom of his evergreens melt into the bushes, with a breath of the warm mist drifting through it. That plants the tree on the ground instead of letting it stand on stilts.

The small lavender hump on the far right horizon, just behind the pine's foot: it's a pale, cool pink, lighter than the orange sky around it. Anything standing between us and a setting sun goes darker than the sky behind it. Perhaps glaze it into a dusky blue-violet a touch darker than the sky beside it, with soft edges that fade into the haze, to match the far tree line under the sun.

The open water along the bottom edge, below the gold column and across the lower right: it stays one even plum all the way down. Picture it deepening gently toward the bottom edge and the lower corners into a rich plum-indigo, with one or two long, faint, rose-tinted sideways sheens across it. Water nearest us reflects the dark sky high overhead, and a darker frame at the bottom pushes the glow farther away and makes it hotter.
visions.keep: The smooth, ringless bloom around the small near-white sun, the crisp flat knife cuts just under it, the glassy smooth lake, the feathered gold column that melts away with no teeth, the hazy blue-violet far tree line with rounded tops, the gold-bellied clouds near the sun, the soft blurred headland reflection, the cabin's lit window and the violet-to-crimson-to-orange sky. My last note on the pine's straight trunk line (and its hard line in the reflection) still stands as an offer if it speaks to you.
